title: Chapter 75 — The Principles of Ethical Influence
intro: Reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity — the aligned versions that serve the customer.

sections.title: Influence Is Not Manipulation
sections.content:
Influence has a bad reputation because it is often taught as manipulation. The principles themselves are neutral — they describe how humans naturally make decisions. Using them ethically means aligning them with the customer's best interest.

Reciprocity: give value first. Help them genuinely and they will want to work with you.
Commitment: the Little Yes technique — small agreements build toward the big decision.
Social proof: 'this is our most popular model in this category' helps customers feel confident.
Authority: your expertise — earned through knowledge and verified with honesty.
Liking: rapport. People buy from people they like.
Scarcity: real urgency when it exists. Never manufactured.

sections.title: The Line Between Influence and Manipulation
sections.content:
The test is simple: would the customer thank you for using this technique if they knew you were using it?

Helping them narrow options through expert advice? They would thank you. Creating fake urgency about inventory you know is fully stocked? They would not.

Every technique in this program passes that test. If it does not, do not use it.

sections.title: Coaching Rule
sections.content:
When evaluating influence techniques, ask:

Does the salesperson use influence to serve the customer — or to serve themselves?
Are urgency and scarcity claims real and verifiable?
Does the customer feel helped — or manipulated?
Would the customer thank the salesperson if they knew the technique being used?
